newsitem.title: UK: British committee discusses fear of cloning.
newsitem.headline: British committee discusses fear of cloning.

text.p: A British government-appointed committee charged with keeping an eye on cloning and other genetic issues held its first meeting on Thursday, and its chairman said fears over a cloned sheep would be high on the agenda.

With concern mounting following the successful cloning of a sheep, the government's science minister sought to reassure the public about the implications of such research, saying it was being closely watched and regulated.
Ian Taylor said the Human Genetic Advisory Commission would be sure to keep the public informed.

"For those who fear that science fiction will come true, they should be clear that a broad range of regulatory controls have been put in place to prevent what is undesirable becoming a reality," the minister said in a statement.

News that scientists in Scotland had cloned an adult sheep rattled nerves all the way from U.S. President Bill Clinton to Nobel Peace Prize winner Joseph Rotblat, with both urging close monitoring of such science.
"The reporting of the remarkable breakthrough achieved at the Roslin Institute risked confusion between science and science fiction," Taylor said.
Sir Colin Campbell, a legal philosopher, chancellor of the University of Nottingham and chairman of the new committee, said he was certain these fears would be discussed.
"We are bound to talk about cloning today," he told BBC radio. "It would be perverse of us not to talk about it."
He said the committee, which was meeting for the first time mainly to set its agenda, would also discuss the implications of genetic testing for insurance, employment and health care.

Insurance companies have stopped short of requiring testing for genetically linked diseases like Huntington's disease, which brings early death -- but British insurers now require people who have been tested to tell them the results.
There are fears that people with genes that could predispose them to disease will be discriminated against.

This week, fears focus on the possibilities opened by cloning experiments. The researchers who cloned the sheep admit it could now become possible to clone a human being, although they denounced anyone who would try.
Campbell said his group would consult another government panel, the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority, on whether current laws banning human cloning were adequate.

"Above all we ought to tell the truth. We ought to say where there are wonderful promises and excitement and contributions to health care, but we also ought to point out where there are terrible dangers," he added.
"Science in this country and science in every other country will not stop and we cannot stop it."

Taylor said he had discussed Britain's extensive network of panels and committees that watch and discuss science with ministers from the United States, France, Germany, Japan, Canada and Italy, and said they had admired it.
"As long as we keep a close eye on genetics and encourage a full and open debate on the new findings, there is much about which to be optimistic," Taylor said.
"Research should help provide answers to some of the mysteries of biology -- how cells specialise, the implications for ageing, and abnormal change in cancers and inflammatory disorders."
